results.title: GDPR Data Governance: Build a Privacy-First Data Strategy in 2026
results.content: # GDPR Data Governance: Build a Privacy-First Data Strategy in 2026. Under the GDPR, strong data governance is critical: it aligns day‑to‑day data management with GDPR principles like transparency, accuracy, accountability, and data minimization. Companies that treat GDPR data governance as a foundation for privacy not only stay compliant but also gain a competitive advantage through greater data privacy and customer trust. In this article, we will understand what data governance is and why it matters to remain compliant under the GDPR, key components of data governance, its challenges, benefits and much more. ## **What Is Data Governance and Why It Matters for GDPR**. Data governance is the organizational practice of managing data quality and security and using it through defined roles and rules. It typically involves a framework of policies, processes, and controls to oversee data accuracy, lineage, access rights, and lifecycle management. ## **The Role of Data Governance in GDPR Compliance**.

results.title: GDPR Data Retention: Compliance Guidelines & Best Practices
results.content: To achieve GDPR compliance, you’ll need to understand these data retention requirements. Our guide explains GDPR data retention requirements to help you achieve and maintain compliance with the privacy regulation. Once you’ve organized your data, you should “*clearly define retention periods based on processing purposes, regulatory requirements, contractual needs, and storage limitation principles*,” Harmeling says. As Harmeling says, “*The GDPR requires businesses to ensure that customer data they store and process was obtained with explicit and informed consent*.” In other words, if you haven’t obtained each user’s permission — or the data processing doesn’t fall under one of the other considerations listed above — you can’t justify collecting or retaining data for any period. The GDPR does not explicitly provide retention guidelines, as how long companies can and must retain data depends on a number of factors, like processing purposes and if they change, and other regulatory requirements that may affect retention periods, like those governing healthcare or finance.
